Backpropagation on an Inference-Only NPU: Pretraining VKORE-46M-NPU From Scratch

Community Article Published
October 14, 2026 Upvote 12 VIDRAFT_LAB SeaWolf-AI FINAL-Bench
Most neural processing units (NPUs) in the market are inference accelerators. The usual assumption is that you can serve on them, maybe quantize for them, but you cannot train on them, and certainly not pretrain a model from scratch. FINAL-Bench/VKORE-46M-NPU is a small, deliberately simple model released to show the opposite: a transformer pretrained from scratch, with real backpropagation, on a first-generation inference-only NPU.
This article is a technical walkthrough: why NPU training is hard, how the model is built, how the run was validated against a GPU reference, what is shared, and what is intentionally not.

Why "training on an inference-only NPU" is a real wall

If you have only ever trained on CUDA GPUs with PyTorch autograd, it is easy to underestimate the gap. Inference-only NPUs are typically built around assumptions that are convenient for serving and hostile to training:

Static, ahead-of-time compiled graphs. The forward graph is lowered and fused by a vendor compiler. There is no general-purpose autograd tape at runtime; the backward graph is not something the stack produces for you.
Weights as constants. Many inference runtimes bake weights into the compiled artifact. Training needs weights to be mutable buffers with gradient and optimizer state attached.
Reduced precision by default. int8 / int4 / fp16 paths are tuned for forward accuracy, not for the small-magnitude gradient accumulation that training depends on. Naive reuse makes loss diverge.
Optimizer state memory. Adam-style optimizers hold first and second moments per parameter, roughly 2 to 3x the parameter memory, on top of saved activations for backward.
Collective communication. At multi-chip scale you need gradient synchronization (all-reduce, or a lower-frequency scheme) that an inference serving path does not ship.

Put together, this is why "NPUs cannot do backprop, so they cannot train" became a reasonable default belief. The point of VKORE-46M-NPU is to provide a concrete counterexample with a reproducible validation protocol.

The model

The release is intentionally a small, clean decoder-only language model, chosen so the training path is the story rather than the model.

Parameters: ~46M
Architecture: decoder-only transformer, RoPE positional encoding, SwiGLU MLP, RMSNorm, grouped-query attention (GQA)
Tokenizer: character-level
Data: roneneldan/TinyStories (public)
Objective: causal language modeling, trained from scratch (no pretrained weights)
Hardware: a first-generation inference-only NPU released in 2025, 32 chips

Character-level + TinyStories + 46M is a classic proof-of-concept configuration. It keeps vocabulary and data simple so that the question under test is narrow and clean: does the training path actually run, numerically, on this hardware?

The validation that matters: a controlled NPU-vs-GPU comparison

The most important artifact is not a single loss curve. It is a controlled comparison. The same model was trained from scratch twice under identical initialization, data ordering, and schedule, once on the 32-chip NPU and once on a GPU reference.

The two loss trajectories correlate at 0.99.
Throughput (tokens/second) converged to a comparable level.

Why this protocol matters: a falling loss on the NPU, by itself, proves very little. Low-precision or mis-implemented backward kernels can still produce a loss that decreases while quietly following a different optimization path than a correct implementation. The informative signal is agreement with a known-good reference under matched conditions. A 0.99 correlation of the loss trajectory against the GPU run is strong evidence that the backward pass and optimizer updates on the NPU are doing numerically the same work as a standard GPU training step, not an approximation that merely trends downward.
If you are evaluating similar claims from anyone, this is the bar to ask for: not "loss went down on hardware X," but "loss trajectory matches a GPU reference under identical seed, data, and schedule."

It ran on older silicon

A detail worth underlining for anyone planning hardware: this was done on a first-generation 2025 inference NPU, not the newest part. If a first-generation inference chip can carry a from-scratch pretraining run that tracks a GPU at 0.99, the headroom on later NPU generations is the interesting open question.

One accelerator, the full loop

With the training path working, a single NPU deployment can cover what previously required splitting work across inference chips and separate training GPUs:

Pretraining from scratch
LoRA fine-tuning
Inference acceleration (confirmed on general open models, not only this one)
Quantized-model execution and speedup

The team packages these capabilities as a software layer called VKORE. The analogy they use is deliberate: the dominant AI compute platform won not only on silicon but on its software ecosystem, and VKORE aims to be a comparable common acceleration layer for NPUs, lowering dependence on any single accelerator and its software stack.

Using the model

The model is a standard decoder-only LM released with weights and a model card on the Hub, so it loads with the usual transformers path for text generation. It is trained on TinyStories and produces short, grammatical English stories. Treat it as a capability demonstration, not a general-purpose assistant.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "FINAL-Bench/VKORE-46M-NPU"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id)

prompt = "Once upon a time"
ids = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=120)
print(tok.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

(Refer to the model card for the exact tokenizer and generation settings, since this is a character-level model.)

What is shared, and what is not

To be precise about scope:

Shared: model weights, the model card, and the NPU-vs-GPU comparison data.
Not shared: the core training technique and training code, which are patent-pending and kept private for IP protection. The method is planned for a later paper.

That boundary matters for reproducibility: you can load and run the released model and inspect the comparison, but the enabling training kernels are not open. This article does not claim an open-source training recipe; it reports a released model plus a validation protocol.

Honest limitations

46M parameters, character-level, TinyStories is toy scale. This demonstrates the training path, not model quality or downstream performance.
Scaling to larger models and real-world data with quality evaluation (perplexity, downstream tasks) is explicitly the next step, not something claimed here.
Because the core technique is withheld, independent reproduction is limited to the released artifacts.

Why this is interesting anyway

Even with those caveats, "from-scratch pretraining with real backpropagation on an inference-only NPU, loss trajectory matching a GPU reference at 0.99" is a result that is rare in the open literature. It reopens a practical question for the whole ecosystem: if inference accelerators can also carry training, the hard split between "inference silicon" and "training silicon" is softer than assumed, with direct consequences for on-device training, energy per training step, and data-sovereign setups where models are grown on-site rather than in a remote GPU cluster.
Model: https://huggingface.co/FINAL-Bench/VKORE-46M-NPU
If you work on custom autograd backends, low-precision training kernels, or low-frequency gradient synchronization on non-GPU accelerators, the comparison data in the model card is the part worth poking at. Feedback from that angle is welcome.
